title: Trump’s Trillion-Dollar Oil Play: A Trap For Big Oil? | OilPrice.com
text:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy

Simon Watkins is a former senior FX trader and salesman, financial journalist, and best-selling author. He was Head of Forex Institutional Sales and Trading for…

U.S. President Donald Trump’s core vision of the future of global oil and gas is to have as much of that supply as possible coming from his self-proclaimed ‘Americas’ region, which is directly in the U.S.’s sphere of influence. Venezuela is one of the key countries from which this increased production is designated to flow, which is why Washington is focusing so much of its efforts on encouraging heavy investment from American oil and gas giants into the country. It is in this context that very recent changes to Venezuela’s ‘Organic Hydrocarbons Law’ should be seen. But are they ultimately likely to achieve their objectives?

The details of these multiple changes to the law were definitively laid out over the past couple of weeks during and after the ‘Venezuela Global Investment Forum 2026’, which was part of a massive push by state oil firm Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. (PDVSA) to lock in 105 new oil contracts by the end of this year. This was the first time the new government -- following the U.S. removal of former president Nicolás Maduro in January -- had delineated the exact tiered fiscal rates on a major international stage to tempt in global capital, despite the broad framework being technically written in January and clarified with fiscal regulations in July. In broad terms, the message presented by Venezuela’s vice minister of commercial policy, Ricardo Gomez, during and after the investment forum has been that the majority state control model for the oil and gas sector established under former president Hugo Chávez, and continued by Maduro, is over and that company operators can now have exclusive control over assets in the sector. Related: How Iran Just Broke the U.S. Oil Shield In Saudi Arabia Yet Again

A crucial addition here is that Venezuela’s amended Organic Hydrocarbons Law has created new investment opportunities across its oil and gas sector, offering international companies varied contract options for developing heavy-oil reserves, mature fields, offshore gas resources and refining infrastructure. The new legal framework allows international investors to choose between hydrocarbon productive participation contracts, restructured joint ventures with state-owned PDVSA, and direct contracts covering infrastructure and oilfield services. For example, perhaps the most direct investment route for foreign firms into the country’s oil and gas sector is offered by the ‘hydrocarbon productive participation contracts’ (CPPHs). In this structure, a company incorporated in Venezuela operates a designated area at its own cost and risk for 25 years and, with ministerial approval, it will also have the legal right to sell its own share of the produced oil and gas directly to international buyers, completely bypassing PDVSA’s trading desks. This is a huge change from the Chávez/Maduro model, under which only PDVSA or another state-controlled entity had the legal monopoly to market and sell the crude. Under that structure, private partners were forced to let PDVSA handle the sales and then wait to be paid their share of the revenues -- a system that frequently led to foreign firms being trapped by PDVSA’s cash-flow crises, defaults, and the impact of primary US sanctions. This new CPPH model has already been used by Italy’s Eni, which transferred its Junín-5 heavy-oil field (with 35 billion barrels of certified oil in place) to this contract type in September, moving from a minority joint venture position to become the asset’s exclusive operator.

In parallel with the multiple contract types now available, each form will carry with it different combined royalty and tax rates. For example, at the bottom there is a 20 percent rate on investment in new infrastructure and unexplored land for greenfield projects. Next up is a 25 percent rate on Orinoco Belt development for extra-heavy crude oil. A 30 percent rate applies to defunct or heavily damaged non-producing brownfield sites. And at the top, there is a 35 percent rate for investment in existing operational assets in brownfield areas. At the same time, the updated investment framework regulations published in July cap royalties at 30 percent and the integrated hydrocarbons tax at 15 percent. Additionally, qualifying offshore projects and developments incorporating upgrading or refining infrastructure may receive reductions of up to five percentage points.

Looking at the positives first, the revised hydrocarbons framework broadly represents Venezuela’s most aggressive and pragmatically designed attempt to attract foreign investment in decades, offering a highly competitive structure on paper. Capping the integrated hydrocarbons tax at 15 percent and lowering total fiscal rates for trickier greenfield or extra-heavy projects shows the government is directly addressing the historically punitive ‘resource nationalism’ of the Chávez/Maduro era that previously drove foreign oil and gas majors out of the country. The minimisation of state interference by allowing foreign firms like Eni to act as exclusive operators is another positive, as it minimises the risks of domestic corruption in key projects. Similarly beneficial is granting investors the right to market their own share of production, thereby solving the historic cash-flow trap resulting from having to wait for PDVSA to pay them. And finally, tailoring the combined royalty and tax rates to the difficulty of exploring and developing the assets -- and offering a 5 percent discount for infrastructure or offshore gas integration -- creates true project visibility and clarity for extra-heavy oil initiatives.
